chunks: And by this chain of narration, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from more than one [narrator], from Aban, from Abi Maryam, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say:

The shahid (martyr) — if there is still a breath of life (ramaq) in him, he is given ghusl, shrouded (kafan), embalmed (hanut), and the salat is performed over him; and if there is no breath of life in him, he is buried in his garments.

key_terms.أَثْوَابِهِ: his garments — the battle clothes in which the martyr died, in which he is buried without further preparation
key_terms.حُنِّطَ: embalming/perfuming with camphor and aromatic substances (hanutat) — a sunnah rite applied to the deceased before shrouding
key_terms.رَمَقٌ: last breath of life; faint vital sign — the juristic criterion that divides two sets of funeral rulings

ai.seo_question: According to Shia jurisprudence, when is ghusl required for a martyr (shahid) and when is he buried in his battle garments?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes a pivotal distinction in Shia jurisprudence: a shahid found with any remaining breath of life (ramaq) after battle receives full funeral rites — ghusl, kafan, hanut, and salat al-mayyit — identical to those of an ordinary deceased Muslim. If found already dead with no ramaq, he is buried directly in his battle garments, exempt from these rites, honoring the sanctity of his martyrdom.
